claims.text: Single-crystal FeNiCrMn has an FCC lattice in the initial state.
The initial material contains a high density of solute-induced local chemical order or solute clusters.
The initial material contains no pre-existing BCC phase.
The yield strength of single-crystal FeNiCrMn is anomalously insensitive to strain rate from cryogenic to elevated temperatures.
Athermally limited dislocation nucleation at pre-existing solute clusters drives the anomalous strain-rate insensitivity.
Thermally activated dislocation glide is not the dominant mechanism controlling the onset of yielding.
FCC-to-BCC phase transformation is not the dominant mechanism controlling the onset of yielding.
Solute-rich clusters act as strong, athermal dislocation-pinning points.
A critical resolved shear stress must be reached to nucleate dislocations at the proposed clusters.
Dislocation nucleation at the proposed clusters is independent of thermal assistance.
Yielding is controlled by the athermal stress required to overcome either the Peierls barrier or cluster resistance.
Athermal control renders yield strength insensitive to strain rate.
Athermal control renders yield strength insensitive or only weakly sensitive to temperature.
Yield strength will remain nearly constant from 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^3 s^-1.
Yield strength will show weak temperature dependence between 4 K and 600 K.
The predicted response applies across crystal orientations provided that the loading orientation supplies sufficient resolved shear stress on an active slip system.
No FCC-to-BCC phase transformation will be observed at the onset of yielding.
Traditional FCC metals show decreasing yield strength with increasing temperature and increasing yield strength with increasing strain rate because of thermally activated dislocation glide.
Polycrystallinity and extreme strain rates that produce adiabatic heating may cause deviations from the proposed behavior.
Detection of more than 1% BCC phase at the yield point is proposed as a falsification criterion.

contradictions.description: The experiment design specifies testing at a fixed temperature such as 300 K, whereas the falsification rule requires the BCC criterion to hold across all tested strain rates and temperatures. A fixed-temperature experiment cannot evaluate the stated full temperature-domain rule.
